title: With Due Respect (Vol. 1) -- Ch. 6: Can GMA Reign Beyond 2010?
keywords: a deception and a gigantic fraud
unlike Ferdinand Marcos... without martial law
primary_topics: Chapter 6 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 1) -- CJP's July 20, 2008 Inquirer column analyzing whether GMA could legally extend her reign beyond June 30, 2010, concluding: yes, IF Congress, the Supreme Court, the Comelec and the people agree to a revision of the Constitution shifting to a parliamentary system

A first-hand recap of the failed 2006 Charter-change bid (during CJP's term as Chief Justice): the de Venecia-allied 'people's initiative' (Sigaw ng Bayan and Ulap, 6.3 million alleged signatures), struck down 8-7 as 'a deception' and 'a gigantic fraud' because the full texts were not shown and because shifting to a parliamentary system is a 'revision, not a mere amendment' that an initiative cannot accomplish

The new 'weapon of choice' -- the constituent assembly (Con-ass) -- and the pivotal legal question of whether Congress votes jointly or separately on a three-fourths proposal: a joint vote would let GMA's 200-plus House majority prevail even over a unanimous Senate

His forecast that a depleted Supreme Court (the 2006 majority thinned by retirements, with GMA 'winning controversial cases') might validate a joint vote and 'wash its hands' to a manipulable Yes/No plebiscite -- echoing how the Marcos Constitution was 'approved' by a show of hands in 'citizens' assemblies'
sub_topics: The thesis: GMA's term expires June 30, 2010, but she could legally extend her reign IF Congress, the Court, the Comelec and the people agree to revise the Constitution to a parliamentary form

The 2006 'people's initiative': led by Speaker Jose de Venecia's allies, the Sigaw ng Bayan and the Union of Local Authorities (Ulap) gathered '6.3 million' alleged signatures and asked the Court to compel the Comelec to authenticate them and schedule a ratification plebiscite

The 8-7 rejection (Lambino): the Court called the initiative 'a deception' and 'a gigantic fraud' because the signatures were gathered 'without first showing to the people the full texts of the proposed amendments,' and held that a presidential-to-parliamentary shift is a 'revision, not a mere amendment' beyond the reach of a people's initiative

The line-up: the decision was penned by Justice Carpio (joined by Ynares-Santiago, Gutierrez, Austria-Martinez, Carpio-Morales, Callejo, Azcuna, and CJP himself), with the dissent by Justice Puno (joined by Quisumbing, Corona, Tinga, Chico-Nazario, Garcia and Velasco); three of the eight (Gutierrez, Callejo, Panganiban) have since retired

Why not initiative or Con-con again: a people's initiative is 'problematic,' and a constitutional convention is 'tedious' and risky given GMA's low popularity -- so the Palace's likely vehicle is the constituent assembly (Con-ass)
The Con-ass mechanics: Congress proposes a revision 'upon a vote of three-fourths of all its Members,' ratified by majority in a plebiscite held 60-90 days after approval

The decisive joint-vs-separate question: if the two houses vote jointly (senators' and representatives' votes added together), GMA's ruling coalition (200-plus of the 240 House members) could reach three-fourths 'even if all the senators would align with the House's puny minority'; the Senate seems willing to convene (Pimentel had proposed a federal system)

The Court and the plebiscite: with the 2006 majority 'decimated by three retirements (four by February 6, 2009)' and GMA 'lately... winning controversial cases,' the Court might validate a joint vote and let a plebiscite decide -- a vote 'easy to manipulate' (Yes/No), recalling the Marcos Constitution 'approved by a mere raising of hands' in 'citizens' assemblies' and validated by 'a compliant Supreme Court'

The timeline and endgame: congressional approval by Dec. 31, 2008, a Court decision by June 30, 2009, a plebiscite in September 2009, and a May 2010 election for a new Parliament -- with GMA taking a parliamentary seat in Pampanga and becoming prime minister in a Lakas-Kampi-dominated Parliament; the closing question: can GMA, 'unlike Ferdinand Marcos,' extend her reign 'without martial law'?

stances.claim: GMA could legally remain in power beyond June 30, 2010 only by revising the Constitution to a parliamentary system -- and only if Congress, the Supreme Court, the Comelec and the people all concur; a people's initiative is foreclosed because a system shift is a 'revision, not a mere amendment,' as the 2006 Lambino ruling held (8-7).

stances.claim: The Palace's viable vehicle is a constituent assembly, where the decisive legal question is joint vs. separate voting: a joint three-fourths count would let GMA's 200-plus House majority prevail even over a unanimous Senate -- a reading a depleted, GMA-favorable Court might validate before passing the question to a manipulable Yes/No plebiscite.

stances.claim: Such a plebiscite would be 'easy to manipulate,' as the Marcos Constitution was 'approved by a mere raising of hands' in 'citizens' assemblies' and blessed by a compliant Court -- so the Comelec's (and Namfrel's and PPCRV's) integrity in counting and guarding the votes would be critical.

notable_anecdotes: A Chief Justice's first-hand account: CJP recounts that the 2006 'people's initiative' was struck down 8-7 during his own term, and names himself among the majority -- a rare insider's recap of how 'a deception and a gigantic fraud' was rejected.

The amendment-vs-revision linchpin: he stresses that shifting from a presidential to a parliamentary system is a 'revision, not a mere amendment,' which a people's initiative cannot accomplish -- the doctrinal heart of the case.
The joint-vote arithmetic: he shows how, with 200-plus of 240 House members, GMA's coalition could reach a three-fourths 'vote of all Members' in a joint session 'even if all the senators' opposed.

Raising of hands: he recalls that the Marcos Constitution was 'approved by a mere raising of hands during citizens' assemblies,' a 'scandalous voting process validated by a compliant Supreme Court' -- a warning about a manipulable plebiscite.

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 6 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 1), CJP's July 20, 2008 Inquirer column, asks whether GMA could legally extend her reign beyond June 30, 2010, and answers: yes, but only by revising the Constitution to a parliamentary system, and only if Congress, the Supreme Court, the Comelec and the people all agree. He recaps, as a first-hand participant, the failed 2006 Charter-change bid during his term as Chief Justice: the de Venecia-allied 'people's initiative' (the Sigaw ng Bayan and Ulap, with 6.3 million alleged signatures) was struck down 8-7 in Lambino as 'a deception' and 'a gigantic fraud' -- the signatures gathered 'without first showing to the people the full texts' -- and because shifting to a parliamentary system is a 'revision, not a mere amendment' beyond the reach of an initiative (Carpio for the majority, which included CJP; Puno in dissent). With the initiative foreclosed and a constitutional convention too 'tedious,' he predicts the Palace's vehicle will be a constituent assembly (Con-ass), where the decisive legal question is whether the two houses vote jointly or separately on a three-fourths proposal: a joint count would let GMA's 200-plus House majority prevail 'even if all the senators' opposed. He forecasts that a Supreme Court thinned by retirements -- and with GMA 'lately... winning controversial cases' -- might validate a joint vote and 'wash its hands' to a Yes/No plebiscite that is 'easy to manipulate,' recalling that the Marcos Constitution was 'approved by a mere raising of hands during citizens' assemblies,' validated by 'a compliant Supreme Court.' Laying out a timeline (congressional approval by December 2008, a Court decision by mid-2009, a plebiscite in September 2009, and a 2010 election for a new Parliament in which GMA takes a Pampanga seat and becomes prime minister), he closes with the question that frames the next column: can GMA, 'unlike Ferdinand Marcos,' extend her reign 'without martial law'?
